findings.impact: Whoever controls this app (its maker, or anyone who breaches the maker) can use the access listed as the accounts that granted it, without their password or second factor, until the grant is removed.
not_checked: When each app was authorized or last used, and what it did with its access, were not checked.

remediation.summary: Confirm someone in the company chose this app and still needs it. If not, remove its access: an administrator can block it under Security → Access and data control → API controls → Manage Third-Party App Access, and each person can remove it at myaccount.google.com/permissions. If it is needed, configure it deliberately on that page: Limited or Specific Google data where it still works, Trusted only if it must reach services you restricted. Trusted widens what the app may reach; it does not limit it, and this finding stays open either way. Prefer a version that asks for less (for example, access to its own files instead of all of Drive). To keep it as it is, accept it by its client id.

findings.title: A third-party app holds broad access to Workspace data
why_here: admin@example.com is a super administrator and granted this app the scope drive: whoever controls the app can use those scopes as admin@example.com, though not that account's other administrator rights.

notes.detail: Returned credential permissions are unknown; effective permissions were not tested.
domains: observed 2; organizational units: observed 3; accounts: observed 6. Inventory alone does not assess account security or administrator access.
scheck could not identify the Google account used for this run. Information from earlier Workspace reads was not used in this report.

The separate token scheck used for the app check holds admin.directory.user.security, which also lets it revoke app access and app passwords, read or create backup codes, sign people out and turn off 2-step verification. scheck sent only the declared reads; effective access was not tested. If you will not run the app check again, remove that permission from the credential's domain-wide delegation entry or consent.

Checked: the apps each account authorized with its Google account and the access Google reports they hold. Not checked: domain-wide delegation, service-account keys, apps an administrator installed for everyone from Marketplace (they may not appear as a person's grant), app passwords, when each app was authorized or last used, and what any app did with its access.

1 app holds scopes scheck does not classify and none it classifies as broad, so it was not judged: "Google Chrome" (77185425430.apps.googleusercontent.com). Its name is chosen by whoever registered it. Check under Security → Access and data control → API controls → Manage Third-Party App Access in the Admin console that someone chose it.

Mail forwarding was not checked. It finds mailboxes that send copies of mail to outside addresses, a common way an attacker keeps reading someone's mail after the password is changed. It needs a Google service account with domain-wide delegation for gmail.readonly, which can read every message; most small companies do not have one, and whoever manages your Google setup (often your IT provider) would create it. scheck signs in as each active mailbox and reads only its forwarding settings and filters, never a message. Whoever approves access to staff mailboxes must approve it and add authorization.mailboxes (asset, by, date, expires) to the engagement file first, then run with that service account's key file and SCHECK_WORKSPACE_PROFILE=directory_oauth_mail.
